title: Good zeal (ch. 72)
hookLine: bear one another's weaknesses of body and character with patience

lines: NEAR THE END OF THE RULE.
cards: Zeal has a mixed reputation. A zealous fan, a zealous inspector, a zealous neighbor with a clipboard and opinions about your lawn. Fire, yes, but often the kind that burns other people.
Near the very end of his Rule, after chapters on prayer, work, food, sleep and punishment, Benedict stops to talk about zeal. He doesn't tell his monks to have less of it.
He says there are two kinds, and they lead in opposite directions. Today: good zeal.

teach.h: A BITTER ZEAL AND A GOOD ZEAL.
teach.b: Chapter seventy-two is short, and it opens with the contrast. There is a bad zeal of bitterness, Benedict says, which separates a person from God and leads toward hell.
And there is a good zeal, which separates a person from vices and leads toward God and everlasting life. Same energy, opposite ends. The bitter kind keeps a list of everyone else's faults.
The good kind is what monks should practice with the warmest love, and his list of what it looks like is almost all about other people.
First, outdo one another in showing honor. That echoes Saint Paul in the Douay-Rheims: "Loving one another with the charity of brotherhood, with honour preventing one another."
Preventing is an old sense: going ahead, getting there first.

teach.h: BEAR WEAKNESS OF BODY AND OF CHARACTER.
teach.b: Then the line today is built on: bear one another's weaknesses, of body or of character, with the greatest patience. Of body: the brother who snores, who's slow, who's sick again.
Of character: the one who interrupts, who sulks, who is exactly as irritating today as yesterday. Benedict doesn't say fix them or report them. He says bear them.
Paul again: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." No one should chase what seems best for himself, but what is best for someone else.
And the chapter ends: prefer nothing whatever to Christ, and may he bring us all together to everlasting life. Benedict's last picture of heaven includes the snorer.

how: Benedictine communities read the Rule aloud in portions through the year, and chapter seventy-two on good zeal is often cited by monks and oblates as a summary of how to live together.

o: an eager love that honors others and bears their faults
a burning wish to suffer hardship for God alone
a strict eagerness to correct other people's faults

s: Benedict tells his monks to have less zeal
he names two kinds, a bitter one and a good one, and asks for the good kind with the warmest love.
the chapter asks monks to seek what is best for someone else
no one chases what seems best for himself, but what is best for another.
"preventing" in the Douay-Rheims means stopping someone
it's an old sense: going ahead of, getting there first.

games.q: you live with the same brothers for life, and one of them has a habit that grates on you every single day. what does chapter seventy-two ask?
o: correct him until the habit stops.
keep your distance so it doesn't bother you.
bear it, with the greatest patience.
games.why: Benedict asks monks to bear one another's weaknesses of body or character with the greatest patience, and to outdo one another in honor.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose small, repeated habit wears on you, and notice the bitter zeal rising, the urge to correct or keep score.

Then, without excusing anything, set the weight on your shoulders for a moment and carry it, and perhaps notice one weakness of your own that someone carries for you. If you pray, hold that person before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Good zeal. In Benedict's Rule, the fire that leads away from vice and toward God, and shows itself in honor and patience toward others. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: good zeal, the subject of chapter seventy-two.

carryVoice: Your line: bear with each other. Good zeal shows itself as honor and patience. Go gently.

sources.q: Loving one another with the charity of brotherhood, with honour preventing one another.
Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ.
